title: Dedicated lane reservations and gradual throttle matrix for tenant isolation
creator: Ethan Collins
description:
Summary:
We need a predictable, minimally invasive mechanism to guarantee baseline throughput for Dedicated customers while allowing safe backfill and graceful degradation when capacity is constrained. This ticket implements a lane-based reservation system plus a gradual throttle matrix that enforces per-tenant floor and slope policies rather than hard-cut preemption.

Goals:
- Provide per-tenant reserved lanes (token buckets) that guarantee a configurable minimum throughput and a bounded latency tail under normal contention.
- When utilization exceeds physical capacity, apply a decay-based throttle matrix (configurable slopes) to reduce throughput proportionally across tenants while prioritizing SLA-bearing reservations.
- Support controlled backfill of unused reservation tokens to improve utilization without compromising guarantees.
- Expose simulator harness and an observability surface (Grafana panels + traces) to validate behavior before rollout.

Acceptance criteria:
1) Implementation of lane-reservation controller with the following controls: reservation_size, refill_rate, burst_credit_limit, backfill_policy (none|aggressive|decay-weighted).
2) Throttle matrix engine that accepts a tenant priority vector and a slope profile to compute per-tenant throttle multipliers in O(n) time for each policy update.
3) Simulator reproduces at least three real-world contention shapes (steady oversub, bursty arrival, multi-tenant ramp) and outputs expected latency/throughput curves; artifacts for each run saved to notebooks.
4) Integration tests that run on a 4-node GPU testbed validating no tenant sees >2x increase in p95 latency under controlled overload compared to baseline.
5) Console metrics and alerting configured: reserved_utilization, backfill_rate, throttle_multiplier, fairness_index; runbook updated.

Design notes and trade-offs:
- We avoid hard preemption because it causes unpredictable failure modes for stateful traces (long KV caches). Instead the decay-based matrix reduces per-tenant effective concurrency gradually, favoring customers with higher contract weight.
- Backfill increases utilization but may cause short-term oscillations; we bias backfill toward low-latency partitions and use a dampening window to stabilize.
- Implementation will be controller-first (control-plane only) with a lightweight runtime admission hook that applies multiplier tokens on request admission. Full pathway requires a small cross-team change in the serving runtime to accept multiplier overrides from the control plane.
- Complexity vs observability: we will keep the throttle function deterministic and monotonic to make SLO reasoning easier.

Rollout plan:
- Phase 1 (sim + unit tests): land simulator and unit tests behind feature flag. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/redwood-inference/pull/4821.
- Phase 2 (canary control-plane): enable lane reservations on a subset of Dedicated clusters, observe reserved_utilization and fairness metrics for 2 weeks.
- Phase 3 (runtime opt-in): small change to serving runtime to accept multiplier; opt-in for a low-risk customer cohort.
- Phase 4 (wider rollout): increase coverage, enable conservative backfill. Each phase gated by automated acceptance tests and manual SRE review.

Open questions:
- Should reservation tokens be billable differently when backfilled? (billing + product discussion required).
- What is the right default slope for the throttle matrix across enterprise vs PLG tiers?
- How to reconcile lane reservations with existing burst credits architecture?

Next steps:
- Finish simulator harness and publish notebooks.
- Review API surface for reservation configuration with PM and billing.
- Coordinate with runtime team to add the multiplier admission hook (small API change).
